en: Dhammasaṅgaṇī 2:
Niddesa 2.3 Nikkhepakaṇḍa (The Section on Enumeration)
2.3.3. The Exposition of Pairs from the Suttas (Suttantikadukanikkhepa) 2.3.3.1.
The Pair Concerning the Portion of True Knowledge (Vijjābhāgīduka) Which phenomena belong to the portion of true knowledge?
States associated with clear knowledge—
these states partake of clear knowledge.
Which states partake of ignorance?
States associated with ignorance—these states pertain to ignorance.
2.3.3.2. The Pair on the Simile of Lightning.
Which phenomena are like lightning?
Wisdom in the three lower noble paths—
these phenomena are like lightning.
Which phenomena are like a thunderbolt?
The wisdom in the path of arahantship above—
these phenomena are like a thunderbolt.
2.3.3.3. The Foolish.
Which phenomena are foolish?
Shamelessness and lack of moral dread.
These states are foolish.
All unwholesome states are foolish.
Which states are wise?
Moral shame and moral dread—
these states are wise.
All wholesome states, too, are wise.
2.3.3.4. The Black Dyad.
Which phenomena are black?
Shamelessness and lack of moral dread.
These phenomena are dark.
All unwholesome phenomena are dark.
Which phenomena are bright?
Moral shame and moral dread—
are these states white?
All wholesome states, indeed, are white.
2.3.3.5. The Pair on Burning.
Which phenomena are burning?
Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
These phenomena are burning.
All unwholesome phenomena are burning.
Which phenomena are not burning?
Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—
these phenomena are not conducive to remorse.
Indeed, all wholesome phenomena are not conducive to remorse.
2.3.3.6. The Dyad of Designation (Adhivacanaduka) Which phenomena are designations?

Whatever is the reckoning, the common usage, the description, the conventional expression, the name, the naming, the designation, the linguistic term, the phonetic expression, and the verbalization of those various phenomena.
These phenomena are designations.
All phenomena whatsoever are the pathways of designation.
2.3.3.7. The Dyad of Etymological Explanations.
What are the phenomena that are linguistic expression (*nirutti*)?
Whatever is the reckoning, designation, description, common usage, name, naming, denomination, linguistic expression, phrasing, and utterance of those various phenomena—
these phenomena are linguistic expression.
All phenomena are the path of linguistic expression.
2.3.3.8. The Dyad of Designation:
Which phenomena are designations?
Whatever is the reckoning, designation, description, conventional usage, name, naming, denomination, expression, phrasing, or utterance of those various phenomena—
these phenomena are designations.
All phenomena indeed are the domain of designation.
2.3.3.9. The Dyad of Name:
Therein, what is name?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, the aggregate of consciousness, and the unconditioned element.
This is called name.
Therein, what is form?
The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
This is called form.
2.3.3.10. The Pair on Ignorance (Avijjāduka).
Therein, what is ignorance?
That which is ignorance, non-seeing... [as before] ...the shackle of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root—this is called ignorance.
In this context, what is craving for existence?
Whatever desire for existence among the states of existence … [as above] … whatever clinging to existence—this is called craving for existence.
2.3.3.11. The Dyad on Views Concerning Existence.
In this context, what is the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*)?
"The self and the world will exist"—any such view, any inclination toward a view, ... [as before] ... any inverted grasp:
this is called the view of existence.
In this context, what is the view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*)?
"The self and the world will not exist"—any such view, a resort to views, ... [and so on] ... a perverted grasp:
this is called the view of non-existence.
2.3.3.12. The Pair on the View of Eternalism.
Therein, what is the view of eternalism?
It is the view, the state of view, and so forth, up to the perverted grasp, that "the self and the world are eternal."
This is called the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
In this context, what is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*)?
It is the view, the state of view, and so forth... the grasping through perversion, [which holds]: "The self and the world will be annihilated."
This is called the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi).
2.3.3.13. The Dyad on the View of Finitude:
In this context, what is the view of finitude (antavā-diṭṭhi)?
The view, the resorting to a view, ... the inverted grasp, such as "the self and the world are finite"—this is called the view of finitude.
In this context, what is the view of infinitude?
The view, the resorting to a view, ... [and so on] ... the misapprehension that "the self and the world are infinite"—this is called the view of infinitude.
2.3.3.14. The Dyad on Views Concerning the Past.
In this context, what is the view concerning the past?
Any view, any resort to views, ... [and so on] ... any inverted grasp that arises with reference to the past—this is called the view concerning the past.
In this context, what is the view concerning the future?
Any view, any resort to a view, ... [and so on] ... any inverted grasp that arises with reference to the future:
this is called the view concerning the future.
2.3.3.15. The Pair of Lack of Moral Shame (Ahirikaduka) In this context, what is lack of moral shame (*ahirika*)?
That which does not feel shame at that for which one ought to feel shame; that which does not feel shame regarding the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
This is called moral shamelessness (*ahirika*).
In this context, what is moral recklessness (*anottappa*)?
That which does not feel dread where one ought to feel dread; that which does not feel dread at the attainment of evil, unwholesome states.
This is called lack of moral dread (*anottappa*).
2.3.3.16. The Pair on Moral Shame (*hirī*):
Therein, what is moral shame (*hirī*)?
That which feels shame regarding what should be felt shameful about, and feels shame regarding the attainment of evil, unwholesome states—
this is called *hirī*.
In this context, what is *ottappa*?
That which one feels shame for when there is a reason to feel shame, that one feels shame for the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states—this is called moral dread (*ottappa*).
2.3.3.17. The Dyad on Refractoriness (*Dovacassatāduka*)
In this context, what is being difficult to speak to?

When one is being spoken to in accordance with the Dhamma, being difficult to speak to, the state of being difficult to speak to, the quality of being difficult to speak to; taking up a contrary position, persisting in opposition, lack of respect, disrespectfulness, absence of reverence, and lack of deference—this is called being difficult to speak to.
In this context, what is association with evil friends?

Those persons who are faithless, immoral, unlearned, stingy, and lacking wisdom— their cultivation, close cultivation, thorough cultivation, honoring, frequent honoring, devotion, devoted service, and following after them in their ways—
this is called association with evil friends.
2.3.3.18. The Pair on Being Easy to Speak To.
Therein, what is being easy to speak to?

When one is being spoken to by a fellow practitioner of the Dhamma, it is being easy to speak to, the state of being easy to speak to, the quality of being easy to speak to; it is the absence of hostility in grasping, the absence of opposition, constancy, respectfulness, reverence, the state of being reverential, and the state of being deferential.
This is called being easy to speak to.
In this context, what is friendship with the virtuous (kalyāṇamittatā)?

Those persons who are endowed with faith, possessed of virtue, learned, generous, and wise—the associating with them, frequenting them, attending upon them, honoring them, revering them, devotion to them, intimacy with them, and being devotedly attached to them—this is [friendship with the virtuous].
This is called having virtuous friends.
2.3.3.19. The Pair on Skill in Offenses:
In this context, what is skill in offenses?
There are five classes of offenses; there are seven classes of offenses.
Skillfulness regarding these offenses—that which is wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called skillfulness regarding offenses.
In this context, what is skillfulness regarding the emergence from offenses?
It is that wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view which constitutes skillfulness regarding the emergence from those offenses.
This is called skillfulness regarding the emergence from offenses.
2.3.3.20. The Dyad on Skillfulness in Attainment In this context, what is skillfulness in attainment?

There is an attainment with directed thought and evaluation; there is an attainment without directed thought and with only evaluation; there is an attainment without directed thought and without evaluation.

That which is skillfulness regarding those attainments—wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called skillfulness regarding attainment.
In this context, what is skillfulness regarding emergence from attainment?

That wisdom which is skillfulness in emerging from those attainments, understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called skillfulness in emerging from attainment. 2.3.3.21.
The Dyad on Skillfulness in the Elements (Dhātu-kusalatā-duka).
In this context, what is skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātukusalatā*)?
It is the eighteen elements: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element...
The tongue-consciousness element, the body element, the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element.

That wisdom regarding these elements which is skillfulness in elements, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called skillfulness in elements.
In this context, what is skillfulness in attention?

That which regarding those elements is skillfulness in attention—wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called skillfulness in attention.
2.3.3.22. The Dyad on Skillfulness Regarding the Bases (Āyatana-kusalatā-duka).
Therein, what is skillfulness regarding the bases?
The twelve bases: [list follows].

The eye base, the form base, the ear base, the sound base, the nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the flavor base, the body base, the tangible-object base, the mind base, and the mental-phenomena base.
That wisdom which is skillfulness regarding these bases, that understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called skillfulness regarding the bases.
In this context, what is skillfulness regarding dependent origination?

With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises.
With craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
The wisdom, understanding, ... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding that—this is called skillfulness in dependent origination.
2.3.3.23. The Dyad on Skillfulness in the Possible.
In this context, what is skill in the causal basis (*ṭhānakusalatā*)?

Whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states—that is the "basis. The wisdom regarding that, the understanding... [as before] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called skill in the causal basis.
In this context, what is skillfulness regarding the impossible?

Whatever states are not causes or conditions for the arising of certain other states—that is the "impossible. The wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding that—this is called skillfulness regarding the impossible.
2.3.3.24. Uprightness (ajjava).
What therein is uprightness?
That which is uprightness, lack of crookedness, absence of deviousness, and lack of insincerity.
This is called uprightness (*ajjava*).
In that regard, what is gentleness (*maddava*)?
It is that which is softness, gentleness, lack of harshness, lack of rigidity, and a humble mind.
This is called gentleness.
2.3.3.25. The Dyad on Forbearance:
Therein, what is forbearance?
That which is patience, forbearance, endurance, absence of harshness, absence of ill-will, and serenity of mind—
this is called patience (*khanti*).
In this context, what is gentleness (*soracca*)?
That which is bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, and both bodily and verbal non-transgression—
this is called gentleness.
Furthermore, the entire restraint of virtue is gentleness.
2.3.3.26. Kindness of Speech (Sākhalya).
Therein, what is kindness of speech?
It is that speech which is harsh, rough, bitter to others, offensive to others, bordering on anger, and conducive to lack of concentration.
Having abandoned such speech as that, he speaks such speech as is harmless, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many people,
and dear to many people; therein lies his gentleness of speech, his amiability of speech, and his lack of harshness of speech.
This is called courtesy.
In this context, what is hospitality?
There are two kinds of hospitality:
There is welcoming with material gifts and welcoming with the Dhamma.
Here, someone is a welcome-giver, either by means of material gifts or by means of the Dhamma;
this is called "welcoming."
2.3.3.27. The Dyad on the Unguardedness of the Sense Faculties.
Therein, what is the unguardedness of the sense faculties?
Here, a certain person, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics.

If, while dwelling with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—were to flow in upon him, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the faculty of the eye;
he does not achieve restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … [and so forth] …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one seizes upon its signs and its secondary characteristics.
If one dwells with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[arise].

If, when these unguarded sense-bases are left unprotected, evil and unwholesome states such as covetousness and dejection were to flow in, he does not practice for their restraint; he does not guard the mind-faculty, nor does he achieve restraint over the mind-faculty.
This lack of guarding, lack of protection, lack of defense, and lack of restraint regarding these six faculties—this is what is meant by that.
This is called lack of restraint in the doors of the sense faculties.
In that regard, what is lack of moderation in eating?
Here, someone, without reflecting and without wise consideration, consumes food for the sake of sport, intoxication, adornment, and beautification.
Whatever lack of contentment, lack of moderation, and lack of reflection there is regarding food—that is called immoderation in food.
2.3.3.28. The Dyad on Guarding the Doors of the Senses.
In this regard, what is the guarding of the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, someone, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells with the eye faculty unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has seen a form with the eye, there should arise in him covetousness or dejection, which are worldliness-mental states that have not yet arisen, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the eye, he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one dwells with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in after him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
This guarding, protecting, and protection of these six faculties is called restraint.
This is called guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
In this regard, what is moderation in eating?
Here, someone partakes of food with wise reflection:
"Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for beautification, but only for the endurance and maintenance of this body,
for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling."
Whatever contentment, moderation, and reflection there is regarding food—that is called moderation in eating.
2.3.3.29. The Tetrad on Forgetfulness of Mindfulness (Muṭṭhasaccaduka).
In this context, what is forgetfulness?
That which is lack of mindfulness, lack of recollection, lack of attention, lack of mindfulness, lack of a refuge, lack of retention,
loss, and oblivion— this is called forgetfulness.
In this context, what is lack of clear comprehension (*asampajañña*)?
That which is ignorance (*aññāṇa*), non-seeing (*adassana*) … [and so on] … the snare of ignorance (*avijjālaṅgī*), delusion (*moha*), the root of unwholesomeness (*akusalamūla*)—
this is called lack of clear comprehension.
2.3.3.30. The Dyad of Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension.
Therein, what is mindfulness?

That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness, individual mindfulness, mindfulness, the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of not losing, the state of not forgetting, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness.
This is called mindfulness.
In this context, what is clear comprehension?
It is that which is wisdom, understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
This is called clear comprehension.
2.3.3.31. The Pair on the Power of Reflection:
Therein, what is the power of reflection?
That which is wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—
this is called the power of reflection.
In this context, what is the power of cultivation?
The cultivation, development, and frequent practice of wholesome states—
this is called the power of development. Furthermore,
the seven factors of enlightenment are the power of development.
2.3.3.32. The Pair of Serenity and Insight.
Therein, what is serenity?
That which is the stability of the mind … [as above] … right concentration.
This is called serenity (samatha).
In that regard, what is insight (vipassanā)?
It is that wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
This is called insight (vipassanā).
2.3.3.33. The Dyad of the Sign of Serenity (samathanimittaduka):
Therein, what is the sign of serenity?
That which is the stability of the mind … [and so on] … right concentration—
this is called the sign of serenity (*samathanimitta*).
In this context, what is the sign of exertion (*paggāhanimitta*)?
That which is the mental arousal of energy …pe… right effort—this is called the sign of exertion.
2.3.3.34. The Dyad on Exertion.
In this context, what is exertion?
That which is the arousal of mental energy …pe… right effort—
this is called exertion.
In this context, what is non-distraction?
That which is the stability of the mind … [as previously described] … right concentration—
this is called non-distraction.
2.3.3.35. The Dyad on Failure in Virtue.
Therein, what is failure in virtue?
It is bodily transgression, verbal transgression, and bodily-verbal transgression.
This is called failure in virtue.
All immorality is also failure in virtue.
In this context, what is failure in view?
There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no oblation; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; and there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge.
‘They themselves, having directly known the world through higher knowledge, declare it’—such a view, such a resort to views... such a perverted grasp:
this is called failure in view.
All wrong view is failure in view.
2.3.3.36. The Pair on Perfection of Virtue:
Therein, what is perfection of virtue?
That which is bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, and both bodily and verbal non-transgression—
this is called the accomplishment of virtue.
Furthermore, the entire restraint of virtue is the accomplishment of virtue.
In this regard, what is the perfection of view?
There is giving; there is sacrifice; there is offering; there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done;
there is this world; there is the other world; there is mother; there is father; there are beings of spontaneous birth.

"There are in the world recluses and brahmins who have gone the right way, who have practiced rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
Such wisdom, such understanding... [as before] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called the faculty of wisdom.
This is called the accomplishment of view (*diṭṭhisampadā*).
All right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is the accomplishment of view.
2.3.3.37. The Dyad on Purity of Virtue (*sīlavisuddhiduka*).
In this context, what is purification of virtue?
It is non-transgression by way of body, non-transgression by way of speech, and non-transgression by way of both body and speech—
this is called purification of virtue.
All restraint of virtue is purification of virtue.
In this context, what is purification of view?
It is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, the knowledge in conformity with the truths, the knowledge of one possessing the path, and the knowledge of one possessing the fruit.
2.3.3.38. The Pair on the Purification of View (Diṭṭhivisuddhi-kho pana-duka) Furthermore, as for "the purification of view":
it is that wisdom, understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view.
And "exertion for one who has seen [the truth]" refers to that mental application of energy … pe … right effort. 2.3.3.39.
The Dyad on the Grounds for Arousing a Sense of Urgency.
“Agitation” means:
the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of illness, and the fear of death.
“An occasion for agitation” means:
Birth, aging, sickness, and death.
And for one who is stirred, there is appropriate striving:
here a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.

He makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

One exerts the mind, strives; for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen, one generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives.
2.3.3.40. The dyad of unwholesome states regarding lack of contentment.
"And dissatisfaction with wholesome states" means:
the desire for more in one who is not satisfied with the cultivation of wholesome states. "And non-retrogression in striving" means:
[the state of not turning back from exertion].

That which is the careful performance, the constant performance, the steadfast performance, the non-contraction of one’s mode of life, the non-laying aside of zeal, the non-laying aside of the burden, the practice, the development, and the frequent cultivation of wholesome states. 2.3.3.41.
The Pair on Clear Knowledge (*Vijjāduka*): Clear knowledge (*vijjā*) is—
The three true knowledges:

the knowledge of recollecting past lives is true knowledge; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is true knowledge; the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is true knowledge.
Regarding "liberation":
Two kinds of liberation:
the inclination of the mind and Nibbāna.
2.3.3.42. The dyad of knowledge of destruction.
Knowledge of destruction is the knowledge of one possessing the path.
Knowledge of non-arising is—
The knowledge of one who possesses the fruit.
The Section on Exposition is finished.
